DRDO signs first high-value deep-tech contract with startup for quantum project
DRDO has signed its first high-value deep-tech agreement with Zero mK India to develop a 20 mK dilution refrigerator for quantum applications. The project is meant to boost indigenous quantum and cryogenic capabilities while reducing reliance on imported systems.
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has signed its first high-value deep-tech project agreement with a start-up under the Technology Development Fund (TDF) scheme for the indigenous development of a 20 millikelvin (mK) dilution refrigerator for quantum applications.
The agreement was signed in New Delhi between the Director, TDF, and Zero mK India Private Limited, a start-up based in Alwar, Rajasthan.
The project is the first high-value agreement under the Rs 500 crore corpus approved by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh for deep-tech and cutting-edge projects.
FOCUS ON QUANTUM TECHNOLOGY
A dilution refrigerator is a specialised cryogenic system capable of achieving extremely low temperatures in the millikelvin range. Such ultra-low temperatures are essential for the operation and testing of several quantum computing platforms and associated quantum technologies.
The indigenous development of a 20 mK-class dilution refrigerator is aimed at strengthening India's capabilities in quantum technology, advanced cryogenics and strategic technologies.
The project also aligns with the National Quantum Mission and is expected to contribute to the development of a self-reliant, quantum-ready ecosystem.
By developing the technology domestically, the project will help reduce dependence on imported cryogenic infrastructure and strengthen India's domestic quantum technology ecosystem.
RAJNATH SINGH CONGRATULATES TEAMS
Rajnath Singh congratulated DRDO, the industry partner and all stakeholders associated with the project. He expressed confidence that the partnership would set an important precedent for future DRDO-industry collaborations in emerging technology domains.
Defence Secretary and Secretary, Department of Defence R&D, and DRDO Chairman Rajesh Kumar Singh also congratulated the teams involved and wished them success in achieving the project objectives.
Director General, Micro Electronic Devices & Computational System and Cyber Security (DG MCC), Director General, Technology Management (DG TM), Director, Solid State Physics Laboratory (SSPL), and other stakeholders were present at the signing.
The project is being monitored, mentored and supported by the Director, SSPL, and his team.

indian-startups-9f5738cb15.headline: Amazon India To Invest $3 Bn In Quick Commerce Arm By 2030: Report
indian-startups-9f5738cb15.fulltext: Ecommerce giant Amazon India reportedly plans to invest $3 Bn (₹28,790 Cr) to expand its quick commerce business, Amazon Now, over the course of next four years. Sources told Reuters that the ecommerce giant will invest $1 Bn in the vertical by the 2027-end, and an additional $2 Bn by 2030. According to the report, Amazon plans to utilise the fresh proceeds to add new dark stores, strengthen inventory management software at stores, deploy AI tools for demand prediction and expand product mix. The focus will be on stocking daily essentials rather than iPhones, added a source. Another source reportedly added that the ecommerce major is looking to expand its dark store network to around 1,300 stores by April 2027 from 750 currently. Amazon India first launched ‘Now’ in Bengaluru in June 2025 and later expanded the service to parts of Delhi in July 2025 and subsequently to Mumbai. While the platform has been comparatively late in entering the quick commerce market, it is picking up momentum. In April this year, Amazon India’s vice president of operations Abhinav Singh, in a blog post, said that the company would invest ₹2,800 Cr (around $300 Mn) to expand its quick commerce vertical and strengthen its logistics network. Notably, this is not the first time that the ecommerce giant has poured in capital into the country in the past year. Last year, Amazon India had announced a ₹2,000 Cr investment to add 17 new fulfilment centres, six sortation centres, and 75 last-mile delivery stations across India. Prior to this, it had also committed an investment of $35 Bn across its India businesses till 2030 to help boost its cumulative exports from the country to $80 Bn by 2030 The investment comes amid rising competition in the quick commerce segment. While the likes of Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto continue to dominate the segment, the entry of new players has intensified the fight. From Walmart-backed Flipkart’s Minutes to Reliance’s JioMart, deep-pocketed giants are aggressively attempting to capture a larger piece of the pie. The new entrants are spending heavily to expand their dark store networks to compete with early movers. For instance, Flipkart Minutes has scaled to 1,000 dark stores across 130 cities, with brokerage UBS estimating that the platform could add another 1,000 dark stores by mid-2027 ahead of the Big Billion Days sale of 2027. Meanwhile, the biggest incumbent Blinkit continues to lead the category with over 2,600 dark stores across 300 cities. Zepto and Instamart, on the other hand, operate over 1,100 fulfilment centres each. At the heart of all this is the homegrown quick commerce ecosystem, which as per Inc42 data, is projected to become a $40 Bn market opportunity by 2030.

indian-startups-84d3327747.headline: UPI MDR Needed To Fight Cyber Threats With AI: NPCI Chief Dilip Asbe
indian-startups-84d3327747.fulltext: A market-driven economic model for UPI is essential to fund escalating cybersecurity, scalability, and infrastructure costs, UPI operator NPCI’s MD and CEO Dilip Asbe said. Speaking at the 13th SBI Banking & Economics Conclave 2026, Asbe defended the move to introduce merchant discount rate (MDR) charges on UPI. The MDR regime will come into effect from October 15. Asbe said that the tools currently available to attackers are more powerful than those deployed within parts of the payments ecosystem. He added that banks and payments companies would need to continuously invest in AI to protect their systems and retain users’ trust. “The ability and the tools with the hackers are really very powerful compared to what we could actually use inside. And somewhere AI is fairly expensive to use, and we’ll have to continue to invest, use AI to make our systems fully protected... (so that) the trust in the payment system is fully maintained. So again, a lot of investments will be required on that,” he said. His remarks came days after NPCI introduced an MDR framework for select P2M UPI transactions. Under the new framework, eligible UPI merchant payments exceeding ₹2,000 will attract an MDR of 0.4%, capped at ₹300 per transaction. Transactions in certain categories, including fuel, railways, telecom, insurance, and capital markets, will attract lower or fixed charges. Asbe said the cost of maintaining and expanding the payments infrastructure has risen sharply. He claimed that certain server hardware that cost around ₹20 Lakh a year ago now costs nearly ₹1 Cr. The NPCI chief estimated that the new UPI MDR framework could generate ₹13,000 Cr to ₹15,000 Cr during its first year. Asbe also said that the growth of digital payments penetration has slowed because of insufficient investment across the ecosystem. Payment companies have already announced fresh investments following the introduction of the new MDR framework. PhonePe today said it would hire more than 20,000 frontline sales personnel and deploy more than 50 Lakh payment devices over the next one year to scale digital payments in rural areas. The Walmart-owned fintech major cited the MDR framework as one of the factors enabling it to make long-term investments in merchant onboarding and payment infrastructure. Meanwhile, Pine Labs announced plans to deploy 10 Lakh soundboxes across India to widen UPI acceptance. “We wanted to invest back into the payments ecosystem as new monetisation opportunities emerged,” Pine Labs CEO Amrish Rau said. Most UPI Transactions To Remain Free Asbe said the new MDR policy has been designed to shield consumers and small merchants from additional costs. Around 96% of UPI transactions by volume and 75% by value will remain outside the charging framework. Besides, about 75% of merchants accepting UPI payments have never received a single transaction exceeding ₹2,000 and, therefore, will remain unaffected by the MDR. Businesses processing more than ₹1,000 Cr in digital payments annually are expected to contribute around 80% of total MDR collections. Another 10% would come from merchants processing more than ₹1 Cr annually, according to Asbe. As these merchants already accept credit cards and pay higher MDR fees for doing so, NPCI believes they are unlikely to pass on the additional cost of MDR on UPI to the consumer. Asbe acknowledged that merchants accounting for the remaining 10% of the chargeable payment value might attempt to pass the cost on to customers. “The remaining 10%, yes, there is a possibility, and the banks, NPCI, the acquirers, and the payment aggregators will have to work towards ensuring that the charges are not passed back,” he said.

global-economics-5c3ab3cf46.headline: India-US trade deal ‘done and dusted’, execution awaits competitive advantage: Goyal
global-economics-5c3ab3cf46.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-5c3ab3cf46.fulltext:
The trade pact between India and the US is "done and dusted" and will be executed once the United States gives India the right competitive advantage over its competitors in the American market, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Thursday.
India and the US in February announced finalisation of the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement (BTA). However, changes in the tariff landscape in the US have led to further negotiations on the pact.
He said that India has finalised nine free trade agreements, "and I include the US, which is almost done and dusted”.
“We have to find the right comparable competitive advantage over our competitors, so that we can quickly execute the agreement,” the minister added.
These remarks come ahead of Goyal's visit to the US for the G20 Trade Ministerial, to be held in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, from September 30 to October 1.
He will also hold a bilateral meeting with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and the progress of negotiations for the pact is expected to be taken up during the deliberations between the two leaders.
INDIA-EU FTA
Goyal also highlighted the negotiating gains secured under the India-EU trade agreement, particularly in response to new European climate and trade regulations like the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and Deforestation Regulations.
He added that India has secured additional steel quotas for domestic exporters and a USD 500 million commitment on climate finance, with more such support expected in the future.
“Even now when they (EU) wanted to restrict steel exports, we have extracted our pound of flesh and safeguarded so many of our agriculture and other sectors and we got a huge extra steel quota. We got another USD 500 million commitment on climate finance. It is the beginning; there will be much more coming,” Goyal said.
India has secured zero-duty market access for over 90 per cent of its steel exports to the European Union (EU) under the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA), with opportunities to export up to 2.8 million tonnes (MT) of steel under various quota arrangements.
Talking about the EU regulations, he said the number has increased to 73, but these would provide huge business opportunities to Indian industry.
“The more they regulate and overregulate and create hurdles for their businesses, the EU is going to get wedged out of the business. Their automobile will never be able to compete with ours with all those regulations. Their roads and infrastructure are going to be so expensive that tolls will rise, housing will become expensive due to restrictions on steel and cement, import quotas and import duties of 50 per cent.
“At the end of the day, the cost of living will become expensive (in Europe), salaries will have to go up, production will have to go up. This will give India a cost advantage. They will have no choice but to manufacture in their trusted geography where their technology is not stolen, their IPR and investments are safe and that is what India offers," he said.
OTHER FTAs
The minister informed that negotiations are progressing with several other trading partners for FTAs.
Canada is making fast progress, the minister said, adding he held a meeting with Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu last week in Mumbai and both sides resolved issues to bring greater political heft to the negotiations.
"When ministers get into the act, then we conclude agreements," he said.
On Mexico, he said the Terms of Reference (ToR) for negotiations had been finalised and the Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal is expected to travel to Mexico next week to take forward the process and launch the negotiations.
The first round of negotiations with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) is scheduled for October, he said. The Terms of Reference of the FTA were signed in February this year.
On trade agreements with Chile and Peru, Goyal said that the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with Chile may happen soon, but with Peru it may not happen due to a lot of competition and competitive interests.
These developments are important as India is seeking to expand its network of FTAs on account of increasing uncertainty at the tariff front and non-tariff barriers.
Goyal said India's FTAs would ultimately provide preferential access to markets accounting for about 75 per cent of global GDP, underscoring the government's strategy of using trade agreements to widen market access for Indian exporters.
CHINA
Criticising earlier governments for engaging in the RCEP negotiations, he said it was an FTA between India and China.
The RCEP (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership) agreement was negotiated among 10 ASEAN members (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam) and their six free-trade pact partners: Australia, China, India, Japan, South Korea and New Zealand.
India in 2019 decided not to join the mega free-trade agreement RCEP as the pact was not addressing its concerns and since then there has been no change in that position.
He said that India already had a trade pact with Asean, Japan, and South Korea and it was negotiating at that time with Australia and New Zealand.
“China was the only other country. So, effectively, RCEP negotiations that we entered into voluntarily would have given us an FTA between India and China," he said.
DIRECT SHIPPING ROUTE
He said it is a challenge which India has and it will only be resolved with two major factors.
"We are looking at massive changes in our maritime regulatory infrastructure and ecosystem by which more and more companies would want to flag their vessels in India. We will provide the best registry in the world for people who flag their vessels. We are working on that; it's a work in progress," he said.
Published on September 24, 2026

ai-eb461d26ec.headline: Australia to investigate if OpenAI hack of government health website broke the law
ai-eb461d26ec.fulltext:
An OpenAI model hacked into an Australian government website, the country’s prime minister Anthony Albanese said Wednesday, in the first publicly reported case of an AI model hacking into a government’s systems.
Albanese said that there would “obviously be legal consequences” following the breach, and that OpenAI faces a government investigation into how its unreleased models gained access to reams of bulk health data information.
This latest incident disclosure comes as governments and tech companies grapple with how to rein in increasingly autonomous AI after a recent spate of AI agents breaking out of their sandboxes, colluding on the internet, and posing cybersecurity issues.
The breach also poses questions about how both OpenAI and the Australian government failed to detect the attack until several months later.
During a Wednesday news briefing at the U.N. General Assembly, Albanese said that the breach began on June 18, but that OpenAI did not notify the government until September 10.
OpenAI only became aware of the incident in August when it turned up during a broader, companywide review of agents behaving in unintended ways, according to an OpenAI spokesperson who reached TechCrunch via email.
The unspecified OpenAI agent obtained both public and nonpublic files from Services Australia, which administers Australia’s universal healthcare scheme. While the prime minister said there is no evidence that any citizens’ personal information was leaked, OpenAI said that the information the agent reached included aggregate health statistics and internal file names.
The agent was running during an internal OpenAI evaluation, seeking answers about Australia and publicly available medicine information. At the Medicare portal, the agent encountered repeated blocks but found ways around them.
Albanese told reporters that the model “didn’t accept no for an answer,” and added that the model had actively written data to the government’s database, rather than just accessing it, indicating the possibility that the department’s data was modified or muddied.
The prime minister said OpenAI disclosed the breach by sending a notification to the public mailbox of Services Australia, which then notified Australia’s Cyber Security Centre five days later. It’s unclear why there was a delay, but Albanese said he raised the breach directly with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman by stressing Australia’s “extreme concern” about this incident and “disappointment” that OpenAI sat on the information for nearly three months.
“This situation is obviously unacceptable,” said Albanese, making clear that he held the company accountable for both the hack and how slowly it came to light.
Albanese said that the government’s investigation will consider law enforcement and legislative responses to prevent incidents like this one happening again.
Australian media outlet ABC News reports that the latest identified attack may have relied on an earlier breach of a German wiki site, which was used as a staging ground for attacking the Australian government’s website. The AI model agents reportedly used the German wiki to leave notes to be used in later hacks, including a note to obtain data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, a federal agency that publishes national health data. The agency is one of three additional systems that Albanese said may have been breached.
Transluce, a nonprofit AI research lab, separately found public records showing AI agents targeting the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare on June 20 and 21.
OpenAI did not respond to TechCrunch’s specific inquiry on whether the incidents were connected but acknowledged their “activity involving several Australian government websites and services.”
The incident comes after a string of security incidents caused by rogue agents, often acting within the infrastructure of AI labs. In July, swarms of OpenAI agents breached Hugging Face. Since then, more incidents of AI agent hacks from Anthropic, Meta, and Google have been revealed.
OpenAI now says it is conducting an “extensive review of misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and is notifying third parties of potential breaches.

ai-5fbe01394f.headline: ElevenLabs’ CEO on margins, IPO timing, and telling customers they’re talking to a bot
ai-5fbe01394f.fulltext:
ElevenLabs builds the voice layer of AI, the models that turn text into speech that sounds human. Most people encounter it when they’re talking with customer service — often without realizing it. Klarna runs first-line phone support for 35 million U.S. customers on it, for example. So do Deutsche Telekom, Cisco, Adobe, and a growing list of governments. ElevenLabs also sells to creators, who use its platform for audiobooks, dubbing, and music.
It’s not alone in what it does. In fact, it’s increasingly bumping into customers, including Decagon, a conversational AI platform that trained its voice product on ElevenLabs and now competes with it. But its investors don’t seem too concerned. The company, which says it’s pacing at $600 million in annual recurring revenue, is now reportedly valued at $22 billion by its backers, despite being just four years old.
To understand more, I interviewed ElevenLabs co-founder and CEO, Mati Staniszewski, at Nrth in Toronto, a local entrepreneurship conference formerly known as Elevate. We covered a range of topics in a short time, including whether businesses should tell customers when they’re talking to an AI (he thinks they should), and whether he could discuss the company’s gross margins. Unsurprisingly, Staniszewski said he couldn’t discuss them in any detail, but he was clear that he doesn’t mind them getting squeezed even further if it means expanding the company’s market share.
Our conversation follows, condensed and lightly edited. You can check out the full conversation here.
You joined us at TechCrunch Disrupt last year, where you said audio models would be commoditized within a couple of years. How would you rate that prediction now?
There is still a lot of work to be done, and the quality delta you can achieve just on the model level is still significant. If we think longer term, probably three, five years from now, those differences will be smaller. What we’d love to do, and be the first ones to do, is pass the Turing test for conversational AI. You need to combine intelligence, but you also need emotional intelligence. You need to understand the emotions of the other side, to be able to slow down or speak up. That hasn’t yet been done.
What percentage of the business is enterprise now?
We are now $600 million in ARR. Fifty-five percent plus is classic enterprise, and a big percentage of the [remaining] 45% are small and medium businesses, developers, builders, creators.
Like everyone else in AI, you’re increasingly competing with your customers. Decagon trained its voice product on you and now runs queries through its own models.
The lines become more blurry. As we think about model companies, platform companies, application companies, in the past you’d have very clear splits where one starts and ends. Today that line is much more blurry. In Anthropic’s case, what was a model company is definitely a platform and increasingly a wide set of applications. I think this will continue.
Your customers can choose the “reasoning layer” from a menu of options at ElevenLabs. What are you seeing in terms of the use of frontier lab models versus open weight?
It’s less of a binary choice. In customer experience, if you’re calling in and it’s just informational, you’re not executing any actions — you can use a lot of the open source models because your knowledge base defines what a good experience is. But if it’s financial services, you want to be authenticated, you want information about a transaction, maybe a refund. There’s no room for error. Here, frontier models will still lead.
Some of those open-weight models are Chinese. The U.S. government is a customer. European governments are customers. What are those conversations like?
Different. In each deployment, the models and the voices we deploy will depend on the case. If we work with the Polish government or the Brazilian government, they have their own set of requirements. It can be an open-weight model, a closed-source model, their own fine-tuned model. [In Poland] it’s a healthcare case. You have patients booking appointments across the public health system, and 18% never show up. The deployment is agents that call and remind you. They had a set of models optimized on their knowledge, and we integrate while keeping data residency.
Should businesses disclose when someone is talking to an agent rather than a human?
I think there should be disclosure at this time. Currently, people aren’t used to it, and the common pattern is you don’t want to feel cheated on that call. But in five years, when everybody has their own agent working on their behalf, you’ll be calling in and expecting an agent. Then I think we’ll shift as a society. There are good ways of doing it — if there’s a 30-minute wait for a human, offer the customer a choice. In almost all cases, they choose the agent and then they’re surprised by how good the experience is.
What are your gross margins, given what you’re paying for models and inference?
I’m going to give a vague answer. Given we have that research element, we’re able to fine-tune and constrain models in extremely smart ways. But if we can pass on any savings to the customer, we do that. The biggest thing is still proving the value and being there with the customer. So if we can invest and prove that value, we don’t mind the margins going lower to actually benefit together as the value gets created in the next five years.
You have millions of hours of customer service calls. Do you train on them? How much of your training data is synthetic?
In certain companies, we created the models together. They wanted a specific model for their use case. Otherwise, the big part of the training hasn’t been so much the volume of data, it was annotating the data. We have thousands of people internally on a contracting basis helping us annotate not only what was said, but when people were speaking, how they said things, what emotions were used. We had to bring voice coaches in to be able to detect accents accurately.
It’s been reported you’re looking at 2028 for an IPO. Can you confirm that?
We’d love to create a company that stands the test of time. We are preparing the foundation to be able to do it in the next years. But whether we do it will depend on the time and place.
“Years” is very vague.
[Laughs.]
Backstage: Where do you land on whether the frontier labs should slow down?
Everybody is aligned to work together on finding a way to pace. Whether they should be public about it, and how much of the media conversation or regulation it should involve, that’s another topic. But yes, we should all take the right precautions as we deploy the technology. We don’t train the text models and the intelligence side of models, which is the core key of the debate.
Could ElevenLabs be exposed the way Hugging Face was?
We’re a step further, because we don’t deploy self-replicating or recurrent parts of the intelligence of agents. Our technology doesn’t allow you to let agents create more agents. Every customer goes through KYC. Cybersecurity risk is definitely a risk for the wider world, but we have a good set of precautions in place.

The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) made its stock market debut on Thursday, September 24, with its shares listing at Rs 1,800 on the BSE. This is a 0.84% premium over its IPO price of Rs 1,785.

climate-energy-8e98b52237.headline: Interactive: What China’s dozens of ‘five-year plans’ say about climate and energy

Interactive: What China’s dozens of ‘five-year plans’ say about climate and energy
Almost three-quarters of the 72 five-year plans published by China this year include policies or targets related to climate change and energy, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
Five-year plans are an important part of China’s policymaking process, signalling key priorities and setting targets for the coming years.
The highest-level 15th five-year plan, which covers “economic and social development” for the period 2026-2030, was published in March 2026.
The government has subsequently published a number of thematic five-year plans at the national level that are specifically focused on climate and energy.
These include plans on renewable energy, responding to climate change and development of its fossil-fuel industries.
Furthermore, the large majority of national-level plans that are not directly connected to climate change also include climate policies – albeit at different levels of detail.
Carbon Brief has combed through all of the 15th five-year plans issued by central-government ministries that are currently available in public for any mentions of topics related to climate change.
The findings, summarised in the interactive tracker below, show that 54 of the 72 plans published so far include climate policies or targets.
For each plan, the tracker lists the most important targets and primary goals, as well as other notable policies and a link to the full text, or a summary if the full text is unavailable.
Using the tracker
Five-year plans are used to guide economic and social development across China.
The overarching plan is published in March at the beginning of each five-year cycle. It outlines the most important high-level targets and policies across all issues.
After the top-level plan, a series of other five-year plans are then published over a period of months or even years, each focused on individual sectors or themes.
In total, Carbon Brief has tracked the 72 plans published to date which cover the 15th five-year plan period, ranging from topics such as the coal industry and electric vehicles through to accounting methods and tourism.
It still remains unknown exactly how many plans for this five-year period are yet to be published – and on what topics – although Carbon Brief understands that the key plans relating to climate and energy have now likely been released.
The current five-year plan period is viewed as being particularly important for climate action, as it covers the years building up to China’s pledge to peak its carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions “before 2030”.
For each five-year plan, Carbon Brief’s tracker summarises all of the climate and energy targets classified as “primary” goals. (These goals are called 主要目标 in the policy documents.)
These include a combination of both numerical and non-numerical targets.
For example, in the overarching five-year plan, the numerical primary targets include cutting carbon intensity – the emissions per unit of GDP – by 17% across the five-year period.
The targets from the overarching five-year plan, as well as others announced before March 2026 – such as the commitment to cut greenhouse gas emissions to 7-10% below peak levels by 2035 – are the basis for policymaking for the next five years.
However, the sectoral and thematic five-year plans provide more specific targets and detailed policy directions.
Non-numerical primary targets are listed on each card as other primary goals. For example, in the five-year plan for a “national meteorological development” these include “significantly enhanc[ing]” capabilities for monitoring, forecasting and warning of extreme weather, as well as making “major progress” in Earth system forecasting.
Primary goals are policies listed in the first section of the plans, either in the main body of the policy document as aims to be achieved for 2030, or in a table of numerical targets.
For each of the plans, the cards also list other notable policies related to climate change or the energy transition. (For each heading on the cards, the full entry can be viewed by clicking the drop-down arrow.)
Unless otherwise specified, quantitative targets refer to 2030, relative to a 2025 baseline.

UPI: Centre asks banks to ensure MDR charges are not passed on to customers, say sources
ADVERTISEMENT
The central government has asked the banks to ensure that the MDR charges on UPI payments above ₹2000 are not passed on to the customers. Sources pointed out that the government will keep a close watch on this, while also maintaining that around 96% of the transactions will remain unaffected.
"Banks have been advised to ensure that merchants do not pass on MDR charges UPI payments above ₹2000 to customers," said a government source.
Sources said MDR is not tax or a cess or urcharge. "Not a single rupee of MDR goes to the Government of India or the Consolidated Fund of India. MDR stays within the payment ecosystem," sources pointed out.
Sources said the rationale behind introduction of the MDR charges on high value transactions is to make the UPI ecosystem, including servers, payment infrastructure, and fraud prevention more robust.
"This is to make India's indigenous UPI ecosystem financially sustainable over the long term. This will helps fund servers, payment infrastructure, cybersecurity, fraud prevention & customer support," sources said.
Sources said MDR on high value transactions will help expand UPI deeper into rural and semi-urban India.
"This will also bring more citizens and merchants onto UPI. India had 55.49 crore UPI users as of June 2026, leaving substantial room for expansion. This will help in expansion and improve products such as Credit on UPI, UPI 123Pay/feature-phone payments and new payment services," sources pointed out.
Earlier today, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) said any move towards introducing a merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI transactions should not result in additional charges being passed on to consumers, while calling for greater investment from participants across the digital payments ecosystem.
NPCI chief executive Dilip Asbe said the ecosystem has operated with zero MDR on UPI for six years, making any attempt to reinstate the charge a difficult transition. He said participants, regulators, the government and citizens would need to work together to ensure the digital payments system continues to evolve.

work-careers-131f37443b.headline: India Data Centre Hiring Spreads Beyond Tech As AI Infrastructure Demand Grows
work-careers-131f37443b.fulltext:
India’s expanding data centre capacity is creating demand for workers beyond traditional technology roles, even as overall tech-related hiring has weakened in recent months, according to new data from Indeed Hiring Lab.
Data centre-related job postings accounted for 1.3% of all job postings on Indeed in India in August, up from 1% a year earlier and nearly double the share recorded two years ago. The trend comes as growing AI adoption drives demand for larger data centre infrastructure.
KPMG has estimated that data centres could represent a $90 billion opportunity for India by 2035, according to Indeed.
While much of the discussion around AI and employment has focused on automation and its impact on existing roles, the data suggests that AI infrastructure itself is creating another layer of employment demand.
“The expansion of India’s data centre capacity is creating a new layer of employment demand as businesses invest in the infrastructure required to support AI and other digital services,” Callam Pickering, senior economist, APAC at Indeed, said.
Importantly, the demand is not limited to software and IT infrastructure roles. Data centres require workers across engineering, project management, business operations and other functions to build, operate and maintain large-scale facilities.
Data Centre Jobs Extend Beyond Software And IT
Software development accounted for 28% of data centre-related job postings in the 2025-26 financial year, making it the largest category. IT infrastructure, operations and support accounted for another 15.6%, while IT systems and solutions represented 7.1%.
However, nearly half of the roles were spread across non-traditional technology functions. Management accounted for 9.9% of data centre job postings, followed by industrial engineering at 5.8%, sales at 5.2%, electrical engineering at 3.6% and project management at 3.5%.
The distribution reflects the range of skills required to run large-scale data centre facilities, from engineering and infrastructure management to commercial and operational functions.
According to Indeed, the share of data centre-related postings has been trending upward since 2023. A chart included in the report shows the proportion moving from below 1% in much of 2023 and 2024 to above 1.2% in 2026.
Overall Job Market Remains Above Pre-Pandemic Levels
India’s broader hiring market also showed some improvement in August. Job postings on Indeed increased 0.2% during the month, taking the year-on-year increase to 7.4%.
Job postings remained 85% above pre-pandemic levels, although Indeed noted that hiring activity has been volatile in recent months.
The data covers recruitment by companies and organisations in the formal economy and does not represent India’s entire labour market, given the significant size of informal employment. Indeed also noted that its data has a greater concentration in technology, management and sales roles.
The platform said the gradual shift towards formal employment means formal-sector job creation is expected to outpace overall employment growth. Formal-sector roles generally offer greater job security, clearer career progression and higher pay, according to the release.
Healthcare Leads Recent Hiring Growth
The strongest recent hiring growth, however, has not come from technology or data centres. Over the past three months, job postings increased across almost 80% of occupations, with healthcare and other people-intensive roles recording some of the largest gains. Childcare postings increased 27%, nursing rose 23%, pharmacy grew 20% and physician and surgeon roles increased 17%. Dental roles grew 16%, while medical technician postings increased 14%.
This growth was partly offset by declines across several technology categories. IT infrastructure, operations and support postings fell 20% over the past three months, while software development declined 19%. Data and analytics postings fell 14%, and IT systems and solutions declined 7.6%.
Despite these declines, the overall volume of technology postings remains above pre-pandemic levels. Pickering said the recent hiring gains in nursing, pharmacy, childcare and medical roles point to continued demand for services that depend on human expertise and are less easily substituted by technology.
For India’s technology sector, the data centre trend adds another dimension to the employment impact of AI. As companies invest in the infrastructure required to run AI services at scale, employment demand could increasingly extend beyond software development into engineering, operations, project management, sales and other business functions.

work-careers-9a972d7d4b.headline: Entry-level tech jobs in NYC are being cut in half by the AI boom
work-careers-9a972d7d4b.fulltext:
At first glance, the tech scene in New York City appears to be thriving: OpenAI and Anthropic have been putting down roots in the city, while stalwarts of the tech industry like Google now have more than 14,000 employees based in New York. Between 2008 and 2023, tech employment in the city has increased 160%, outdone only by the explosive growth of the tech industry in San Francisco.
But overall job growth in NYC’s tech industry has stagnated in recent years, and there is one area in particular that has experienced a sharp dip: Entry-level tech jobs have taken a significant hit in the years since ChatGPT’s public release ushered in the AI boom.
A new report from the Center for an Urban Future (CUF), a New York-based think tank, found that as of 2022, the number of entry-level job postings in the tech industry has dropped 49%—a bigger decline than in any other sector, even as generative AI has seemingly derailed entry-level hiring across sectors. There continues to be a steady supply of college graduates with computer science degrees, but there aren’t nearly enough entry-level positions available to them.
“The core issue is that employers face an individual incentive to hire workers who already have two or three years of experience,” Eli Dvorkin, editorial and policy director at CUF and one of the authors of the report, said in a recent interview with Searchlight. “But if every employer acts that way, the broader entry-level ecosystem collapses, which ultimately harms employers as well.”
The analysis found that on the whole, the jobs that have seen a marked dip in hiring are those that are most exposed to generative AI. Since 2022, entry-level job postings in roles with high AI exposure have decreased 29% across New York City.
The outlook is not quite as grim across other jobs: Entry-level hiring has remained robust—growing 21%—for jobs that are not especially exposed to AI, according to the CUF report. Even within tech, employers have continued hiring for roles that require expertise in security and data analysis. Entry-level workers with strong AI skills are in particularly high demand, and job postings have actually climbed 20% in over the past four years.
Still, the overall decline in hiring for entry-level tech jobs echoes a broader shift in New York: Since 2022, most industries have seen a steady drop in job postings for entry-level roles.

beyond-your-beat-329d32e27d.headline: How China Thinks About AI
beyond-your-beat-329d32e27d.fulltext:
When I talk to people about AI safety, I often hear this logic:
- America must slow down AI development before we build a machine intelligence that escapes human control.
- But we can’t slow down unless China slows down.
- China won’t slow down.
- Therefore we can’t slow down.
By this logic, the future of AI development—and, according to some, the future of the economy and the entire human race—depends on America’s understanding of China’s approach to artificial intelligence. But I cannot tell you how many times I have spoken to blazingly intelligent people around the AI industry who have told me “Now, I’m not a China expert, but…” and then gone on to defend America’s AI strategy in the context of a subject that they just told me they don’t fully understand.
I myself have never pretended to be a China expert. That’s why this article isn’t written by me, exactly. Instead, I spent the last two weeks calling and emailing a dozen experts on China and AI and reading the primary sources they sent me. Then I organized the most interesting parts of those interviews under seven big questions about China, AI, safety, and what the US government and the AI labs can and should do to protect the world. My summary analysis of the China-AI conundrum is at the bottom of this article.
Q: Do China and the U.S. see AI the same way, or are they telling themselves entirely different stories about the technology?
Some context is useful here before we dive into the interviews. For a long time, several AI experts insisted that China wasn’t “AGI-pilled”—meaning that the nation’s government and labs weren’t devoting significant capital and compute toward the construction of world-leading models with the goal of producing a machine smarter than human experts across domains. But that certainty is weakening. A leaked transcript from a May 2026 closed-door investor meeting revealed that DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng is devoted to building AGI, and Chinese researchers are publishing more papers about what they call “L5” AI—a technology that could “govern” its own self-improvement without human intervention. Tempering these ambitions is the fact that China is significantly behind the US in compute and data center construction, and it’s unclear if the government sees AI as central to future geopolitical dominance as America does.
China regards AI almost polytheistically, as one of many important tech bets, including cars and energy; America treats AI more monotheistically, as the centerpiece of its grand tech strategy
Matt Sheehan, senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace:
China and the U.S. have different stories about AI. Xi Jinping sees artificial intelligence as an across-the-board enabler of a huge number of industries. China’s biggest AI policy in recent years is called the “AI+” plan. It’s AI plus manufacturing, and AI plus scientific research. At this point, it is far and away the technology they care the most about. In the U.S., AGI has always been the anchor for how everybody sees AI. Every development is put into that narrative. Every safety incident and every big math problem solved immediately gets put into the context of “does this mean that AGI is close?” But China evaluates new pieces of evidence without the conclusion in mind. It’s not to say the safety people are wrong. But they’ve been drawn to that conclusion for a long time. China’s political leadership has not.
The West’s AI strategy has been shaped by science fiction
Jordan Schneider, founder and editor of China Talk:
This is sort of a hot take, but I think the people building AI in the U.S., and the West in general, have been deeply shaped by the science fiction stories that they read when they were younger about a post-AGI utopia. I’m thinking of stuff like The Player of Games, and writers like Iain M. Banks. These guys believe that they are building the future that they read about when they were kids. And that shapes the way they talk about the potential of the technology.
China’s labs are getting more and more serious about AGI (artificial general intelligence) and RSI (recursive self-improvement)
Martin Chorzempa, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics:
I’m an outlier in thinking Chinese firms are more AGI/RSI-pilled than most people believe. DeepSeek says its goal is AGI. Moonshot says its goal is AGI and globalization. Other labs’ earnings calls talk about trying to unleash RSI. The Chinese labs see themselves as fast followers. From their perspective, the American labs are dealing with the hard challenges of alignment and security, and the Chinese labs think they can piggyback on that work.
China and America’s economic advantages (e.g., compute vs. robotics) shape their respective views on the future of AI
In her essay “How China Hopes to Build AGI Through Self-Improvement,” Zilan Qian, a program associate at the Oxford China Policy Lab, writes that Chinese researchers tend to imagine AGI emerging slowly through robotics and via feedback from the physical world, whereas Americans are more likely to imagine a sudden and purely software-driven explosion of intelligence via recursive self-improvement. These different attitudes might be shaped by on-the-ground capabilities, such as the fact that China has fewer high-powered chips but has a deep robotics supply chain, whereas the U.S. has abundant compute but weaker on robotics. Here’s Qian:
Chinese scientists’ vision of AGI and self-improvement looks quite different from that of Silicon Valley. Rather than a rapid software-driven intelligence explosion — AI building AI in a recursive loop — Chinese thinking converges on something more embodied: human-level intelligence that requires physical-world interactions…
What matters is not only what Chinese AI researchers and Beijing believe AGI is, but also what happens quietly beneath those beliefs. Just as China sees the future of AI through its manufacturing strength and chip shortage, the U.S., with abundant chips and less manufacturing capabilities, sees a different version. The U.S. and China’s roads to AGI appear to be different, and perhaps the destinations do too. But if each side’s vision of AGI is shaped by what it already controls, then neither is well-positioned enough to recognize what the other is actually building.
Q: Do you buy the premise that the US frontier labs are in a prisoner’s dilemma with China?
The prisoner’s dilemma might be real. “Decisive strategic advantage” is not.  
Matt Sheehan:
The prisoner’s dilemma dynamic is real. At the same time, I have doubts about the claim that once AI passes some threshold of superintelligence, it will give China a “decisive strategic advantage,” which is the term floating around national-security AI circles. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said if we lose AI to China, it’s all over, because once China achieves superintelligence, they can demolish our cyber and nuclear capabilities and put us in a permanent state of subservience. But when you talk to actual nuclear security people, they have a very hard time getting behind that idea. If you’re a country that invents a powerful tool that you don’t understand and don’t know if you can control, is the first thing you do going to be to declare war? I’m not sure about that.
We should think about AI risk like gain-of-function research 
Rush Doshi, former deputy senior director for China and Taiwan on Joe Biden’s National Security Council, currently at Georgetown University and the Council on Foreign Relations:
AI research [is] a bit like gain-of-function research in biology. That kind of research can be dangerous: if you increase the lethality or transmissibility of a virus that you’re studying, and it can be very damaging to everyone if it escapes containment. There’s an element of these models, particularly when it comes to cyber risk, that resembles gain-of-function risk, where the sandbox perhaps takes the place of the biolab. The problem in biology is that you cannot always get countries to stop doing gain-of-function research. So, yes, the world created some standards, but implementation remains a challenge. China, for example, has cut corners with safety in their biolabs.
Q: How does China—and the CCP, in particular—think about AI safety?
Two weeks ago, the New York Times reported that China’s top spy chief warned the state that AI could pose a direct threat to the Chinese Communist Party’s hold on power and “pose a threat to humanity itself.” Many China watchers sent the story to me, suggesting that it proved that China was much closer to the U.S. than it appeared on the issue of not wanting to build AGI/RSI. But I wanted to know more about how Chinese labs and the state really thought about AI safety, so I asked my sources about it.
The Chinese Communist Party has many reasons to accelerate AI, even if they have qualms about safety  
Jordan Schneider, responding in part to the above Times story:
Obviously, an authoritarian government doesn’t want autonomous AI agents running around and taking control away from the state. But China is Leninist, and there is a strain of Leninist thought that isn’t afraid of running the economy as a machine. I think Khrushchev and Brezhnev would have loved to entrust Soviet economic planning to a superintelligent machine. 
There is the military argument: We all know AI can be a powerful weapon. There is the surveillance case: For the CCP, there is something inherently appealing about having an AI-powered panopticon. There is the economic argument. The Chinese economy has been stuck at slow growth for years. The bet Xi has made in the future of the economy is on emerging technologies. If advanced AI holds the potential for China to have widespread productivity growth, he wants that. So, as a literal weapon, as a potential driver of productivity, as a tool for surveillance, and as a point of international prestige, AI is, and will continue to be, very appealing to Xi.
China has a budding AI safety contingent…
Paul Triolo, partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group:
The Chinese safety community cares about AI safety, and is increasingly sophisticated in its assessment of risks from advanced AI. Chinese AI companies increasingly care about safety, as they want to make sure that their models are not misused by bad actors. The Chinese government has been slow to mandate AI safety teams and testing at leading AI companies, in part because of the desire not to overregulate the companies and ensure they are competitive with US leaders. At the same time, the Chinese government would have a hard time mandating safety testing when Chinese companies are already short of advanced compute capacity. So at a minimum, the Chinese government should seek to mandate AI companies have AI safety testing teams, and then possibly provide a national testing platform to ensure there is sufficient compute for safety testing.
… but China’s AI safety community is smaller and weaker than in the U.S.
Matt Sheehan:
China’s AI safety community is small. They have some influential connections and allies. But it’s not like the U.S., for several reasons. First, in China, there is a sense that the party is going to make the big decisions on national security, so the companies feel less personal responsibility [to fixate on safety]. Second, the Chinese labs are behind the frontier labs, so they’re not yet seeing the same capabilities that are scaring Anthropic and OpenAI researchers. Finally, while the Chinese government imposes a lot of requirements on AI companies, the overwhelming majority of those requirements regulate political speech rather than other kinds of risk. It’s mostly about controlling information, not regulating frontier-AI safety.

ai-ab3a59da1c.headline: AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’
ai-ab3a59da1c.fulltext:
Technology experts have warned revelations an artificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s internal systems will not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, on Thursday after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.
OpenAI alerted the government earlier this month to the June hacking via an email to a public-facing address, a situation Albanese called “obviously unacceptable”.
But the Australian Council on AI Strategy chief executive, Anna-Maria Arabia, said the case was unlikely to be an isolated incident.
“All of the evidence shows that our operating systems are vulnerable,” she told Guardian Australia.
“Frontier AI now has capability to expose those vulnerabilities at a rate quicker than we can keep up, quicker than we can patch them.
“When the companies are undertaking tests in what they think are secure environments, and when there are breaches of those environments and these incidences do happen, whether it’s accidental or not, what we’re seeing is the frontier AI capability exposing these vulnerabilities.
“All evidence suggests that there is more of this to come.”
Arabia said Australia needed to quickly enhance capability to detect and report incidents, and the country should host AI training labs here.
Johanna Weaver, Australia’s former chief cyber negotiator at the United Nations, agreed more incidents were inevitable.
Weaver is a member of the advisory board to the minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, and the executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute.
“Cybersecurity experts have been warning that frontier models and AI agents could expose vulnerabilities in critical systems. What we are seeing now is the tip of the iceberg,” she said.
“Governments need to draw a clear line: if companies cannot control their AI systems, they should not release them publicly.”
The US Studies Centre expert Olivia Shen warned AI companies should not be allowed to decide on their own disclosure obligations for hacks and breaches.
“We just don’t know how big the problem is. It could be the tip of the iceberg but, either way, we can’t be ignoring the risk,” Shen said.
“It’s all happening at a time when Australia is designing our national standards on AI. It hasn’t been entirely clear if those national standards were going to be very hyper-focused on datacentres and leave governance questions as a bit of a bolt-on.
“This strengthens the argument that you need to have some pretty clear standards, even just based on mandatory incident reporting, built in.”
Intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is reviewing how prepared the government is to block and respond to hacking by AI. Officials will look at policies around how AI companies should report cyber-incidents to the government, and how cooperative companies should be during and after an attack.
It will also investigate whether the current laws and systems are adequate to stop AI and how government systems can be strengthened.
The shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, called for Australia to develop its own domestic AI capability, instead of relying on the US.
“If there’s rogue AI agents out there, we need to have our own defensive AI agents protecting Australian government data, our private sector and other things that are important to us,” he said.
The Greens demanded Labor call in the new US ambassador, David Brat, to establish what the president, Donald Trump, knew about the attack.
“This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose,” the Greens’ acting leader, Mehreen Faruqi, said.
“The fact that the government did not even know it happened is disturbing.”

health-tech-f6b89ea2cc.headline: STAT+: In radiology, AI is blurring the line between technology development and clinical practice
health-tech-f6b89ea2cc.fulltext:
A decade ago, machine learning scientist and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton made a proclamation that still puts radiologists on edge.
“If you work as a radiologist,” the so-called godfather of artificial intelligence said at a conference, “you’re like a coyote that’s already over the edge of the cliff, but hasn’t yet looked down.” Deep learning was getting so good, so fast, said Hinton, that “people should stop training radiologists now.” In five years — ten, max — AI would do better than radiologists, he predicted.
The clock has run out on that prediction. But the field of radiology isn’t just staring at its shoes, waiting to see how technology upends the profession. Instead, a growing number of radiology practices, in particular outpatient and teleradiology groups, are aggressively embracing AI: developing and acquiring their own tech, deploying it in-house, and marketing their “AI-native” capabilities to radiologist employees and hospital customers alike.

india-deep-tech-90ac7c9a4f.fulltext:
Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has signed the first high-value deep tech project agreement with Rajasthan-based start-up Zero mK India Private Ltd to collaborate for indigenous development of a ‘20 mK Dilution Refrigerator’ for quantum applications. The programme carries a corpus of ₹500 crore and would be funded under the Technology Development Fund (TDF) scheme of the DRDO, the Ministry of Defence said on Thursday.
Dilution refrigerators are specialised cryogenic systems capable of achieving extremely low temperatures in the millikelvin range. Such ultra-low-temperature environment is essential for the operation and testing of several quantum computing platforms and associated quantum technologies.
National Quantum Mission
The indigenous development of 20 mK-class dilution refrigerator aligns with the National Quantum Mission and strengthens India’s capabilities in quantum technology, advanced cryogenics and strategic technologies, contributing towards a self-reliant, quantum-ready ecosystem.
This will contribute towards reducing dependence on imported cryogenic infrastructure and strengthening the domestic quantum technology ecosystem.
The signing of the agreement took place between Director, TDF and Zero mK India Private Ltd, in the national capital. It is the first high value agreement under the ₹500 crore corpus which was earlier approved by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh for deep-tech and cutting-edge projects, the Ministry stated.
Singh complimented DRDO, industry and all stakeholders associated with this important project. He expressed confidence that the partnership will set an important precedent for future DRDO-Industry collaborations in emerging technology domains.
Congratulating the teams associated with the initiative, Defence Secretary and Secretary, Department of Defence R&D and Chairman, DRDO Rajesh Kumar Singh wished them success in achieving the project objectives.
Director General, Micro Electronic Devices & Computational System and Cyber Security (DG MCC); Director General, Technology Management (DG TM); Director, Solid State Physics Laboratory (SSPL), and other stakeholders were present on the occasion. The project is being monitored, mentored and supported by Director, SSPL and his team.

Google's Suncatcher project aims to put AI data centers in orbit powered by solar energy
Google wants to put AI data centers in space. Its "Suncatcher" project would run AI infrastructure in orbit on solar power. On October 1, an experimental satellite called "MVP" is set to launch on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the New York Times reports. The "refrigerator-size satellite" was built and tested at Planet Labs in San Francisco. Google VP James Manyika says it should pack enough computing power to handle basic AI queries from orbit.
SpaceX and Blue Origin are also working on orbital data centers, but the hurdles are massive. Google manager Travis Beals estimates you'd need around 10,000 satellites to match a single 1-gigawatt data center on Earth. There's no air in space for cooling, cosmic radiation can fry chips, and launch costs would have to drop to about $200 per kilogram before the math works out. Jeff Bezos thinks it could take up to 20 years before orbital data centers beat ground-based ones on cost.

indian-startups-33ce2fb576.headline: Ema Raises $77 Mn To Scale Its Universal AI Employee Platform Globally
indian-startups-33ce2fb576.fulltext: Agentic AI startup Ema has raised $77 Mn (over ₹738 Cr) in a Series B funding round led by Bengaluru-based VC firm Creaegis. Existing investors Accel, S32 and Prosus also participated in the round. With the round, the startup has now raised about $140 Mn in funding till date. It claims to have quadrupled its valuation from its $50 Mn Series A round in 2025. It refrained from disclosing its latest valuation. The San Francisco-based startup plans to deploy the fresh capital to scale its go-to-market strategy and expand into new geographies, including Asia Pacific (APAC) and Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA). Ema cofounder and CEO Surojit Chatterjee said, “Enterprises do not need more software. They need outcomes. Our latest funding round will help us drive agentic business transformation at enterprises still stuck in the pilot purgatory.” Founded in 2023 by former Coinbase CPO Chatterjee and former Okta executive Souvik Sen, Ema builds what it calls ‘universal AI employees’ — agentic AI systems designed to plan and execute enterprise workflow. Based in San Francisco, Ema has offices in Bengaluru, London and Vancouver. The startup has nearly 200 employees and has primarily focused on enterprise customers in the US and Europe so far. The SaaS startup currently focuses on automating functions like human resources (HR), information technology (IT) and finance, connecting with more than 250 business applications and systems of record. Its AI Employees can execute tasks across existing enterprise software, check their own work and route sensitive decisions to human employees for approval. Its customers include Wipro, Hitachi, ADP and PwC. "Our customers are not running experiments; they are running their HR, IT and Finance operations on AI Employees at a scale of millions of interactions a year,” Chatterjee said. The fundraise comes as enterprises increasingly move from experimenting with GenAI towards deploying agentic AI systems capable of carrying out business processes autonomously. More and more companies are deploying AI within their workflows to automate tasks and bring down company costs. Unlike conventional SaaS products that provide software tools for employees, Ema is positioning its AI Employees as systems that can actually execute work across the software businesses already use. With more organisations bringing AI into their workflows, instances of mass layoffs within the tech ecosystem have become more prevalent. Recent examples include Amazon cutting 16,000 jobs globally, Oracle laying off thousands of employees amid its AI and cloud infrastructure push, and Meta planning significant workforce reductions as it doubles down on AI. In the Indian startup ecosystem, Livspace cut around 1,000 employees, Innovaccer reduced its workforce by about 350, while GoKwik laid off 100-120 employees as part of an AI-led restructuring. More recently, Uber announced that it is planning to cut 200-250 jobs in India, with its AI Solutions team reportedly among the affected units, while PayPal has laid off around 220 employees in India as part of a global restructuring.
